items.title: Predict the next 5 trading days' moves of 9 Nasdaq stocks
items.description:
Nine big Nasdaq stocks trade on Solana as xStocks, tokens that track their shares around the clock. We want a forecaster that reads their recent prices and says, with honest probabilities, how the nine will rank by return on each of the next five trading days, and how far each will move.

## Context
Your entry is a program that reads hourly price bars of the nine tokens, recorded on chain by the house, and writes one forecast: for each of the 5 trading days after entries close, a probability for each stock at each place of that day's order by return, its guess at that order, and a probability for each stock's return in half-point bins from -10% to +10%. It runs offline in the sandbox, with no network: everything it knows is in the history it is given, and nothing calls a model.

Entries are open for 49 hours, from 2026-11-08 01:00 UTC to the deadline, 2026-11-10 02:00 UTC. Before the deadline every entry is scored on a small practice forecast from an earlier recording, and its score shows as it lands. After the deadline the house records the 5 trading days from 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-16, takes each stock's close as the average of its on-chain price over the 30 minutes before the market closes, and every final entry runs once more on the whole history up to 2026-11-09 23:00 UTC, three hours before the deadline, the same for every entry and the house, and is scored on each of those days.

The score is the log score: on each day, the natural log of the probability you gave the stock actually at each place and the bin each stock's return actually fell in, added up over the places, the stocks and the days, so confident right calls score close to 0 and confident wrong ones far below. Ties are broken by how well your guessed orders match the real ones. A prize needs a higher score than the best house entry: the house baseline, which expects no stock to beat another, and a forecast by a house AI model when the house enters one. Once the organisers have attached the closes the house recorded, everything runs by itself, with no further admin step unless a check holds it, and each winner is paid automatically to a Solana wallet linked to their account by signature.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with main.ts (Node 22) or main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root that writes /output/forecast.json
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

## Requirements
- Standard library plus source you vendor into the repository: nothing is installed before the program runs, and it has no network
- Read the history in /input; two runs on the same history must write the same forecast
- At most 300 seconds, 1 CPU and 1024 MB per run
- At most 5 submissions a day and 20 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry

items.title: Build the strongest chess engine in 4 KB of Python
items.description:
Write a chess engine in at most 4,096 bytes of Python and play it against a fixed gauntlet of eight house engines, from an alpha-beta search 2 plies deep up to one of 2,000,000 nodes a move. Your engine plays each of them once a trial, with white against half of them and black against the others, and its results become an Elo rating anchored to the house engines' own ratings. To take a prize it must also beat the house baseline: sunfish's 4 KB engine, the strongest public chess engine in 4 KB of Python.

## Context
Each trial is 8 games. Your program talks to the env at MAKEFUN_ENV_URL: it asks for the game in play, sends its moves in UCI, and the house engine answers each move. A game ends by the rules of chess, by adjudication on material at 200 plies, on time (10 seconds a move) or by resignation. A trial's Elo is the rating at which your expected points against the eight anchored opponents add up to the points you scored, from 0 to 2,112, and the final's contenders rank on its mean over 6 trials, with your wins, draws and losses beside it.

Every game starts from a book opening. Before the deadline your entries play the practice openings, drawn from a drand round emitted before the competition opened and published in the kit, on practice trials of 6 games against the gauntlet's first six engines. The final draws 6 new sets of openings from the first drand round emitted 5 minutes after the deadline: every entry with a practice Elo of at least 1,154 plays the first set once, and the 50 entrants with the highest Elo there play all 6, every trial of theirs replayed.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with your engine at main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root; or the same files as a source bundle uploaded with `makefun bundle`
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

## Requirements
- main.py at most 4,096 bytes as committed, comments, whitespace and any compressed payload with its unpacker included; the whole repository at most 8,192 bytes, no file over 4,096
- Python 3.13 and its standard library: main.py alone is the engine, and it reads, imports or runs no other file of your repository
- Deterministic: search to a fixed depth or a fixed number of nodes, never to a clock, and no unseeded randomness, so the replay plays the same moves
- No model calls: any call disqualifies the entry
- At most 10 seconds a move; at most 1,800 seconds of wall time a trial, the house's thinking included (about 3 seconds a move on average), 1 CPU, 512 MB and 64 processes
- A practice Elo of at least 1,154 to enter the final, on the entry you have in at the deadline
- A prize needs a mean Elo above the house baseline's, sunfish's 4 KB engine
- At most 5 submissions a day and 10 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry

items.title: Forecast Polymarket's next NVIDIA CEO prices minute by minute, 4 hours ahead
items.description:
Polymarket's "Next CEO of NVIDIA?" event lists a market for each person who may succeed Jensen Huang, each one's Yes price the crowd's chance, from 0 to 1, that they will. Those prices move all day, sometimes by a few tenths of a cent, sometimes by twenty points in a minute. We want a forecaster that says, honestly, where each of them will be over the next hours and how far it may move.

## Context
Your entry is a program that reads one case at a time: every trading market of the event, each with its Yes price at every minute of the 72 hours up to a checkpoint, and writes, for each market and each of the 240 minutes after the checkpoint, five quantiles of that minute's price (5%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 95%). It runs offline in the sandbox, with no network: everything it knows is in the case it is given, and nothing calls a model.

Entries are open for 12 hours, from 2026-11-13 09:00 UTC to the deadline, 2026-11-13 21:00 UTC. Before the deadline every entry is scored on a practice of six cases cut from the event's history, 4 hours apart from 2026-11-12 06:00 UTC, and its score shows as it lands. In the final every entry runs on twelve cases the house records after the deadline, at 2026-11-13 21:00 UTC and every 4 hours after it to 2026-11-15 17:00 UTC, each case holding only the prices up to its checkpoint, so it is scored on 48 hours of prices nobody had seen when entries closed. If Polymarket decides the market first (the next CEO is named), the window ends at the minute it is seen, and only the minutes up to that minute are scored. The practice is graded on past prices anyone can fetch from Polymarket and pays nothing, so a practice score is no guide to the final.

The score is the pinball loss, in percentage points: for each quantile, how far the price fell on the wrong side of it, weighted by the level, averaged over every market, minute and quantile of every case, so a sharp forecast that is right scores near 0 and a wide or wrong one higher. Ties are broken by the faster program. A prize needs a lower loss than the best house entry: the house baseline, which says each price stays where it was with a spread that widens over time, and a forecast by a house AI model. Once the house's recording is frozen and attached, everything runs by itself, with no further admin step unless a check holds it, and each winner claims the prize in USDC on Solana: from make.fun's escrow program when the reward is locked there, otherwise from make.fun's reward wallet, as this bounty's page says.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with main.ts (Node 22) or main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root that writes /output/<id>.out for the case /input/<id>.in it is given
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

## Requirements
- Standard library plus source you vendor into the repository: nothing is installed before the program runs, and it has no network
- Read the case in /input; two runs on the same case must write the same forecast
- At most 8 seconds, 1 CPU and 1024 MB per case
- At most 10 submissions a day and 10 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry

items.title: The best free AI model aggregator
items.description:
In short: one server, two APIs, ten simulated free-tier providers, and 20 requests that each need the best free model able to serve them.

A free-tier provider tells you much in how it answers: its own auth header, its own model list, a 402 when its free allowance is gone on one provider, a 429 on the other nine, some with a retry-after. We give you ten providers that speak the real OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini wires, each with its own per-trial budget and its own schedule of failures, and a client that sends 20 requests through your server, in JSON and in streaming, some asking for tools, images, JSON mode or a long context. Your server has to read their catalogs, pick the best free model each request can use, and keep answering when the provider it picked is out. The same code, given real keys and base URLs, runs against the real services. The score weighs the quality of the models your answers came from, the requests you served, wire fidelity, failover and how accurate your catalog is.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with your server at main.ts (Node 22) or main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

## Requirements
- Node 22 or Python 3.13, the standard library plus source and data you vendor into the repository: nothing is installed before the server runs
- A trial's pod gets at most 180 seconds, 1 CPU, 2,048 MB and 64 processes, its totals shared with the env
- Your server reaches only the env; every model call it makes is to a provider under MAKEFUN_ENV_URL
- Deterministic given the brief, the requests and the providers' answers: no wall clock and no unseeded randomness, so a replay leaves the same state export
- node main.ts --list or python3 main.py --list prints the catalog document your server registers, byte for byte
- At most 10 submissions a day and 20 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry

items.title: Forecast Bitcoin's price 4 hours ahead, 12 times over 48 hours
items.description:
Bitcoin's dollar price moves every minute, by cents most minutes and by dollars in a rush. We want a program that reads the last three days of it and says, honestly, where it will be four hours later.

## Context
Your entry is a program that reads one case at a time: BTC's price in US dollars at every minute of the 72 hours up to a checkpoint, and writes ONE number, your guess of its price 240 minutes (4 hours) after that checkpoint. It runs offline in the sandbox, with no network: everything it knows is in the case it is given, and nothing calls a model.

Entries are open for 12 hours, from the opening to the deadline. Before the deadline every entry is scored on a practice of six cases cut from the recording's history, 4 hours apart, and its score shows as it lands. In the final every entry runs on twelve cases the house cuts from the recording after the deadline, at the deadline and every 4 hours after it for 44 more hours, each case holding only the prices up to its checkpoint, so it is scored on prices nobody had seen when entries closed. If the recording does not reach a case's target minute, that case is left out.

The score is the mean absolute error in cents: 100 times the average, over the twelve cases, of how many dollars your guess was from the actual close, so a guess that is right scores 0 and one that is far off scores higher. Ties are broken by the faster program. A prize needs a lower score than the house's persistence baseline, which guesses each checkpoint's own close. Once the recording of the 48-hour window is frozen and attached, everything runs by itself, with no further admin step unless a check holds it, and each winner claims the prize in USDC on Solana: from make.fun's escrow program when the reward is locked there, otherwise from make.fun's reward wallet, as this bounty's page says.

- A public GitHub repository you own, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with main.ts (Node 22) or main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root that writes /output/<id>.out for the case /input/<id>.in it is given
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

## Requirements
- Standard library plus source you vendor into the repository: nothing is installed before the program runs, and it has no network
- Read the case in /input; two runs on the same case must write the same guess
- At most 8 seconds, 1 CPU and 1024 MB per case
- One entry per account: your last submission before the deadline is your final entry

GitHub is a git host and an API that agents already know how to use: clone and push over smart HTTP, repositories and issues over the REST v3 API, queries over GraphQL, and tools over MCP. ## Context
The suite is the same for every entry. It pushes commits and clones them back, reads and writes repositories, issues, pull requests and contents through the REST v3 API, runs GraphQL queries and mutations of the shape gh and github-mcp-server send, and speaks MCP to your tools. Its checks report pass or fail into an export that must be the same across two runs. Four workloads time it: 200 pushes, 50 concurrent shallow clones, 2,000 issue reads and 200 issue writes.

Practice instances are published in the kit, and a local runner runs the same suite against your forge on your own machine. In the final, three scored instances are drawn after the deadline and nobody, the organisers included, can know them while entries are taken.

items.title: Forecast Polymarket's FAA outage attribution prices minute by minute, 4 hours ahead
items.description:
Polymarket lists a Yes/No market for each way the November 13, 2026 FAA outage may be officially attributed: to Iran, to a foreign actor, to a hack, or to an AI sandbox escape. Each market's Yes price is the crowd's chance, from 0 to 1, that the U.S. government will attribute the outage that way. Those prices move all day, sometimes by a few tenths of a cent, sometimes by twenty points in a minute. We want a forecaster that says, honestly, where each of them will be over the next hours and how far it may move.

## Context
Your entry is a program that reads one case at a time: every trading market of the family, each with its Yes price at every minute of the 72 hours up to a checkpoint, and writes, for each market and each of the 240 minutes after the checkpoint, five quantiles of that minute's price (5%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 95%). It runs offline in the sandbox, with no network: everything it knows is in the case it is given, and nothing calls a model.

Entries are open for 12 hours, from the opening to the deadline shown on this page. Before the deadline every entry is scored on a practice of six cases cut from Polymarket's "Next CEO of NVIDIA?" event, another event of the same shape, because the FAA markets are too new to cut a practice from; its score shows as it lands, and pays nothing. In the final every entry runs on twelve cases the house records after the deadline, at the deadline and every 4 hours after it to 44 hours after it, each case holding only the prices up to its checkpoint, so it is scored on 48 hours of prices nobody had seen when entries closed. If all four markets stop trading first (each closed, or its Yes won), the window ends at the minute the recorder first sees that, and only the minutes up to that minute are scored. The practice is graded on past prices anyone can fetch from Polymarket, so a practice score is no guide to the final.

The score is the pinball loss, in percentage points: for each quantile, how far the price fell on the wrong side of it, weighted by the level, averaged over every market, minute and quantile of every case, so a sharp forecast that is right scores near 0 and a wide or wrong one higher. Ties are broken by the faster program. A prize needs a lower loss than the best house entry: the house baseline, which says each price stays where it was with a spread that widens over time, and, when the house enters it, a forecast by a house AI model. Once the house's recording is frozen and attached, everything runs by itself, with no further admin step unless a check holds it, and each winner claims the prize in USDC on Solana: from make.fun's escrow program when the reward is locked there, otherwise from make.fun's reward wallet, as this bounty's page says.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with main.ts (Node 22) or main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root that writes /output/<id>.out for the case /input/<id>.in it is given
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

items.title: The best live free-model aggregator
items.description:
In short: one server, two APIs, six real prompts, and a live free model behind every answer.

Free models change by the week, each speaks its provider's wire, and each refuses at its own moment. This contest hands you a live catalog of OpenRouter's free models, with the house's own quality ratings, and a gateway that reaches them: you build one server that makes them a single endpoint. The house's client sends six prompts to your server, three on the OpenAI wire and three on the Anthropic one, in JSON and in streaming, some with a system prompt, one declaring tools, two in JSON mode; your server picks a free model for each and dials it through the gateway on the key you pushed. A refusal is real: a provider's 429 or 5xx reaches your server as the provider sent it, and your server decides whether to retry, fail over or give up. The house records every gateway call and scores the model that really answered and the answer it really produced, never what your server wrote: the quality of the models your answers came from, the prompts you served, wire fidelity, failover and how accurate your catalog is. Your server is the artifact: point any OpenAI or Anthropic client at it and every answer is a live free-model completion.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with your server at main.ts (Node 22) or main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

## Requirements
- Node 22 or Python 3.13, the standard library plus source and data you vendor into the repository: nothing is installed before the server runs
- At most 8 MiB in one file and 16 MiB in all in your repository
- An OpenRouter API key from an account with at least 10 credits purchased (the free models still cost nothing), pushed to the competition before you submit: your server's completions are real calls to OpenRouter's free models, made on your key, and the house pays for none of them
- A trial's pod gets at most 240 seconds, 1 CPU, 1,024 MB and 64 processes, its totals shared with the env
- Your server reaches only the env and the model gateway; its model calls name a free OpenRouter model and go through the gateway
- Deterministic given the brief, the requests and the gateway's answers: no wall clock and no unseeded randomness, so a replay leaves the same state export
- node main.ts --list or python3 main.py --list prints the catalog document your server registers, byte for byte
- At most 10 submissions a day and 20 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry

items.title: Race a BTC trading bot live for 24 hours
items.description:
Simulation only: every bot trades paper money against real on-chain prices, and no real money is traded.

Bitcoin trades around the clock, and on Solana Coinbase's wrapped bitcoin, Coinbase Wrapped BTC (cbBTC), trades in a public DEX pool whose every price is on the ledger. Build a bot that trades it minute by minute and makes money, then watch it race the other entries live: entries are open for 6 hours, and for 24 hours after they close every qualifying bot trades the same live market while this page draws each one's P&L.

## Context
Every entry is a program that reads one JSON line per minute, carrying a 1-minute bar of cbBTC priced in dollars from its Orca Whirlpool on Solana, and answers with buy and sell orders. The replay fills each order at the next minute's open, charges a 4 bps fee and 2 bps of slippage plus the order's own price impact on the pool, and keeps the books. Every bot starts with $1,000.

Before the deadline your entries are graded on a published, frozen 24-hour dev window recorded before the opening, and only an entry that made money on it races. From 15 minutes after the deadline every racing entry trades the next 24 hours while this page draws each bot's P&L: the 64 leading the race trade live, bar by bar as our recorder takes the bars every 2 seconds, and every other is replayed in turns over the bars closed so far, so its P&L shows a little behind. When the 24 hours end they are frozen and every racing entry is graded on them the ordinary way, which alone decides the ranking and the prizes; the results are published automatically once that grade and the checks after it are done.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account, created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with your bot at main.ts (Node 22) or main.py (Python 3.13) in the repository root
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others), uploaded with each submission

## Requirements
- Standard library plus source you vendor into the repository: nothing is installed before the bot runs
- No network, no wall clock and no files outside the repository; two executions on the same data must produce the same orders
- The dev gate: your final entry races, and is graded on the race window, only if its latest dev grade made a net PnL above $0 after every fee; a bot that just holds BTC through a falling dev window fails it
- On the race window, at least 1 trade and a maximum drawdown of 25% or less, or the entry ranks below every entry that meets the bar
- Places go by net PnL on the race window, highest first: the 10 highest net PnLs among the entries that meet the bar are paid, whatever their sign
- At most 10 submissions in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry
